Your athlete just finished a set. Here's their biomechanics analysis and rep data. Give three beats in 2-3 short sentences, in whatever order feels natural: one takeaway about the set, the ONE adjustment for the next set (in body units when the ADJUSTMENT gives them), and one specific thing that went well — a CUE OUTCOME where the fix held is the best one. Plain qualitative words: whole numbers only where they help (a rep number, a cm adjustment, a score change), never decimals, degrees or seconds. Open differently than you did after the last set. No humor in this reply — keep it straight, supportive, and forward-looking. Here is the data: Set 1 of 2 just finished: 0 of 3 reps clean. Next up is set 2 of 2. Load: bodyweight. Depth was very consistent from rep to rep. Faults: knees caving in on 3 of 3 reps. This set's focus was knees caving in. CUE OUTCOME: after your cue on knees caving in at rep 1, it still showed on 2 of the 2 reps after. Roughest rep: rep 1 — knees caving in. 
FORM SCORE: 62 out of 100 (depth: 99, trunk: 57, knee: 0, symmetry: 100, tempo: 87) TREND: stable over the set TOP ISSUE: Push your knees out over your little toes the whole way down and up — think spread the floor. ADJUSTMENT: knees pushed out about 8 degrees more LONG-TERM (mention once, briefly, as something to build over the coming weeks — not a fix for the next set): Your knees cave even with a good stance and good ankles, which usually means the side glutes aren't holding them out. Add side-lying leg raises, banded side walks and single-leg step-downs. Never say or imply anything about lower-back tucking (butt wink), upper-back rounding, bracing, or foot arch — the cameras can't see those.
